Market value on January 1 drives the Utah tax bill, and a primary residence is taxed on only 55% of it after a 45% reduction. The rule sits in Utah Code 59-2-103, which sets one uniform rate of valuation for taxable property unless a specific law changes it.

Most Utah homes get the reduction, subject to a few limits.

  • Land counts only up to one acre for each residential unit.
  • A household gets it on a single primary residence. Homes lived in by a tenant as a primary residence are an exception.
  • A property that turns residential after January 1 can still qualify once it is lived in for 183 or more consecutive days that year.
  • Transient use and condominiums in rental pools do not qualify.

Three county offices handle your bill. The assessor sets value, the auditor mails the valuation notice, and the treasurer takes payment. Call whichever one matches your question.

All counties follow the same statewide calendar, but forms, payment portals and office hours differ. Notice rules for tax sales vary by county class: first class counties post on a website and smaller ones use newspapers. Owners of a rural house should look at the county treasurer's page for payment methods and any local deferral process.

Every owner on the assessment roll gets a valuation and tax change notice from the county auditor, mailed by July 22. Utah Code 59-2-919.1 sets the timing: at least 10 days ahead of the county board of equalization meeting and ahead of any taxing entity hearing on a proposed rate increase.

Look on it for the assessor's value, the taxable value, last year's tax, the tax at the current rate and appeal instructions with the deadline. Residential notices add a line about deferral for owners who are 65 or older, disabled, or in extreme hardship. Owners can elect electronic notice, and the county falls back to mail if it can't confirm receipt.

If you're selling, read this notice before listing or signing a contract. The value on it feeds next year's tax bill, and the appeal clock starts when it is mailed.

File your application with the county board of equalization by the later of September 15 or 45 days after the auditor mails the valuation notice, as set out in Utah Code 59-2-1004. Expect a decision from the board within 60 days of the application, though the Tax Commission can extend that.

If the county board's answer isn't acceptable, the next level is the State Tax Commission. Under 59-2-1006, the notice of appeal goes to the county auditor within 30 days after the board's final action. The commission may admit more evidence and adjust the value. It weighs the accuracy and comparability of evidence, including sale prices of comparable property under contract as of the lien date, and offering prices of property that was listed but did not sell.

The commission must decide real property appeals by March 1 of the following year. It also adjusts values when the property deviates by 5% or more, up or down, from comparable properties after an equalization issue is raised.

Tax notices go out by November 1, taxes are due November 30, and a payment that arrives or is postmarked later is delinquent. Here is the calendar a prospective seller needs.

DateWhat happens
January 1Valuation date for market value, and the date the annual tax lien attaches
By July 22Valuation notice mailed by the county auditor
September 15 or 45 days after noticeAppeal deadline to the county board, whichever is later
September 1Common deadline for abatement, senior deferral and exemption claims
By November 1County treasurer mails the tax notice
November 30Taxes due, moved to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday
By December 31Notice of delinquency to unpaid owners
January 31Last day to pay delinquent tax and penalty before interest runs from January 1

Miss the due date and the bill picks up a penalty of 2.5% of the delinquent amount or $10, whichever is greater. Clear the taxes, notice charges and penalty by the following January 31 and the penalty falls to 1% or $10.

After January 31, interest runs on an annual basis from the January 1 following delinquency. The rate is 6% plus the federal funds target rate on that January 1, but never less than 7% or more than 10%, as written in 59-2-1331. Each further year of delinquency adds its own interest until the taxes are paid or the property goes to a tax sale.

Before the delinquency date the treasurer will take partial payments of $10 or more on the current year. Someone paying only part of a bill can say how to divide it among tax, assessments, past-due district fees and other notice charges.

Counties add extra items to the property tax bill called tax notice charges, and these rank equal to the tax. Utah Code 59-2-1317 lists examples such as liens for unpaid municipal water, unpaid abatement fees, special district fees, irrigation district charges and assessment area payments.

Unpaid charges can set a tax sale in motion just as unpaid tax does. The bill has to carry a warning when prior taxes or charges are delinquent on the parcel, plus a notice about assessment area charges that paying one bill may not pay off the full amount owed or release the lien.

The total on the bill may hide some of this. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure that includes charges, interest and penalties before closing.

Counties administer abatements, deferrals and exemptions, and State Tax Commission Publication 36 sets the income and age tests. Current amounts follow.

  • Homeowner low-income abatement: up to $1,412 for owner-occupants with 2025 income under $44,221 who meet an age, disability or prior-credit test.
  • Mandatory senior deferral: for owners age 75 or older with income not over $88,442. It carries interest at half the normal rate and must be renewed yearly.
  • Service-connected disability exemption: up to $535,459 of taxable value on a residence for anyone with at least a 10% service-connected disability.
  • Blind exemption: up to $11,500 of taxable value, with no age or income test.
  • Deadline for most claims: September 1.

A county legislative body can also accept less than the full tax due or defer it when it finds that serves the best interests of the owner, the county and the state, under 59-2-1347. Any deferred amount becomes a recorded lien, bears interest, and is due when the property is sold or otherwise conveyed.

A lien for each year's tax attaches on January 1, which means the closing agent normally pays off any balance from your proceeds after checking the figure with the treasurer.

A change in ownership also triggers a residential exemption check. Under 59-2-103.5, after an ownership interest changes the county assessor sends the owner a notice, and the new owner must return a signed residential declaration within 90 days. A second notice gives 30 more days before the exemption is lost for that year. A seller who stops living in the home should also notify the county board of equalization that the residence no longer qualifies, unless they moved to another primary residence that qualifies.

Three problems come up again and again: a deferral lien, a delinquent bill nobody opened, and an exemption that changed after a transfer. The fix differs for each.

  • Deferral lien: deferred tax plus interest comes due when you sell. Get the balance from the county.
  • Delinquent bill: paying by January 31 holds the penalty at 1%. Otherwise line up a payoff before a tax sale draws near.
  • Lost exemption: file the declaration inside the county's window, or appeal before the September 15 cutoff.
  • Inherited house: bills may keep going to the late owner, so change the mailing address.

When the house also needs work or has turned into a burden, an as-is cash sale can clear these balances at closing without the owner fixing anything first.

faqs.q: When are Utah property taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills are due November 30 (the next business day when that lands on a weekend or holiday). Notices arrive by November 1. Anything paid or postmarked later is delinquent.

faqs.q: What is the Utah residential property tax exemption?
faqs.a: Primary residences are taxed on 55% of market value after a 45% reduction. The break covers up to one acre per unit and one primary home per household.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Utah property value?
faqs.a: Whichever is later: September 15, or 45 days from the auditor's mailing of your valuation notice. You then have 30 days to take a board decision to the State Tax Commission.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for paying Utah property tax late?
faqs.a: The greater of 2.5% of what's late or $10. Paying everything by January 31 cuts that to 1%, and interest from January 1 starts after that date.

faqs.q: Can I defer my Utah property tax?
faqs.a: Some can. Owners 75 and older who meet income tests qualify for a mandatory senior deferral, and counties may allow others. What you defer is recorded as a lien and paid on sale.
